chapters.n: First Kings opens with the mighty David now old and frail, unable to keep warm even under blankets. His weakness creates a power vacuum, setting up a struggle over who will succeed him.

f.g: Advanced in age; David was about seventy (2 Samuel 5:4).
Gat = got; he could not get warm.

chapters.n: His servants suggest finding a young woman to attend and care for him and lie beside him to keep him warm — a remedy known in the ancient world.

f.g: Care for him, look after him; the Hebrew suggests being a nurse or attendant.

chapters.n: They search all Israel and find Abishag from Shunem, a beautiful young woman.

f.g: From Shunem, a village in the Jezreel Valley in northern Israel.
Borders, territory.

chapters.n: Abishag serves as David’s nurse, but the king has no sexual relations with her. The note shows how weak David has become — and her status will matter in chapter 2.

f.g: An idiom meaning he did not have sexual relations with her.

chapters.n: Adonijah, David’s oldest surviving son, decides to make himself king. Like Absalom, he gathers chariots, horsemen, and fifty runners as royal symbols.

f.w: fifty men to run before him

chapters.n: David had never disciplined or questioned him. Adonijah is handsome and next in line after Absalom. David’s pattern of indulging his sons again leads to trouble.

f.w: his father had not displeased him at any time
f.g: David never corrected him.
Very handsome.

chapters.n: Adonijah wins two powerful supporters: Joab, the army commander, and Abiathar, a senior priest who had stood by David for decades.
But other key leaders stay loyal to David: the priest Zadok, Benaiah of the royal guard, the prophet Nathan, and David’s elite warriors.

f.g: Probably royal officials; this Shimei is likely not the man who cursed David.

chapters.n: Adonijah holds a great sacrificial feast at En-rogel, just outside Jerusalem, inviting his brothers and Judah’s royal officials — effectively a coronation party.

f.g: “The serpent’s stone,” a landmark near the spring.
A spring southeast of Jerusalem where the Kidron and Hinnom valleys meet.

chapters.n: He pointedly leaves out Nathan, Benaiah, David’s mighty men, and Solomon — the people he knew would oppose him.
Nathan, the prophet who once rebuked David, now acts to protect God’s plan. He warns Bath-sheba that Adonijah is claiming the throne without David’s knowledge.
Nathan explains the danger: if Adonijah becomes king, Bath-sheba and Solomon could be killed as rivals.
He tells Bath-sheba to remind David of his oath that Solomon would reign after him. This promise is not recorded earlier, but Chronicles confirms God had chosen Solomon.

f.w: Assuredly Solomon thy son shall reign after me

chapters.n: Nathan will follow her in to confirm her words — two witnesses to stir David into action.

f.g: Literally “fill up” or complete your words.

chapters.n: Bath-sheba enters the king’s room. The narrator notes David’s age and Abishag’s presence, a quiet contrast between the aging king and his former vitality.
Bath-sheba bows respectfully, and David asks what she wants.

f.g: Bowed low in honor.

chapters.n: She reminds David that he swore by the Lord that Solomon would be king.
Yet Adonijah is now acting as king without David even knowing.
She describes Adonijah’s feast and lists who was invited — and that Solomon was excluded.
All Israel is waiting for David to declare who will succeed him.

f.w: the eyes of all Israel are upon thee
f.g: In that culture, the reigning king normally named his successor.

chapters.n: Otherwise, when David dies, she and Solomon will be treated as traitors.

f.g: Die.
Literally “sinners” — treated as guilty enemies of the new king.

chapters.n: Right on cue, Nathan arrives while she is still speaking.
Nathan is announced and bows deeply before the king.

f.w: bowed himself before the king with his face to the ground

chapters.n: Nathan asks, with careful tact, whether David has decided that Adonijah should be king.

f.g: A diplomatic question that forces David to state his intentions.

chapters.n: He reports that Adonijah’s guests are already shouting, “Long live King Adonijah!”

f.g: Literally “Let King Adonijah live!” — a royal acclamation.

chapters.n: Nathan, Zadok, Benaiah, and Solomon have all been left out.
Has the king done this without telling his loyal servants? Nathan’s question presses David to act decisively.

f.g: Showed, told.

chapters.n: David calls Bath-sheba back into his presence.
David swears by the Lord, who has rescued him from every trouble.

f.w: that hath redeemed my soul out of all distress

chapters.n: He confirms his oath: Solomon will reign after him, and he will make it happen that very day.

f.g: In my place.

chapters.n: Bath-sheba bows to the ground in gratitude, wishing the king long life.

f.w: Let my lord king David live for ever
f.g: A courtly expression of loyalty.

chapters.n: David summons the three loyal leaders: Zadok, Nathan, and Benaiah.

He instructs them to put Solomon on the king’s own mule — a public sign of royal approval — and take him to the Gihon spring. Centuries later Jesus would enter Jerusalem humbly on a donkey as the true Son of David.

f.g: Jerusalem’s main spring, in the Kidron Valley below the City of David — within earshot of En-rogel.

chapters.n: Zadok and Nathan are to anoint Solomon king, with trumpets and the cry, “Long live King Solomon!” Both priest and prophet take part, giving divine sanction.
Then they are to bring him back to sit on David’s throne. David officially names Solomon ruler over both Israel and Judah.

f.g: Over both the northern tribes and Judah — the whole united kingdom.

chapters.n: Benaiah answers “Amen,” praying that the Lord will confirm the king’s word.

f.g: “So be it; it is true.”

chapters.n: He also prays that the Lord will be with Solomon and make his reign even greater than David’s.
The loyal leaders and the royal guard escort Solomon on David’s mule to Gihon.
Zadok takes the horn of sacred oil from the tabernacle and anoints Solomon. The trumpet sounds, and the people shout their acclamation.

f.g: The tent David had set up for the ark.

chapters.n: Crowds follow Solomon back up into the city, playing flutes and rejoicing so loudly the ground seems to shake.

f.g: Played flutes.
Split, burst.

chapters.n: Adonijah and his guests, just finishing their feast nearby, hear the noise. Joab, the old soldier, immediately senses something is wrong.

f.g: Commotion, tumult.

chapters.n: Jonathan, son of Abiathar, arrives. Adonijah hopefully assumes he brings good news.
Jonathan delivers the crushing news: King David has made Solomon king.

f.g: Truly; or “No! On the contrary.”

chapters.n: He describes the procession, the royal escort, and the king’s mule.
Zadok and Nathan have anointed Solomon at Gihon, and the celebration is the uproar they heard.

f.g: The city echoed with the noise.

chapters.n: And Solomon is already seated on the royal throne.
The officials have congratulated David, praying that Solomon’s name and throne will be even greater than his. David bows in worship on his bed.
David praises God for letting him live to see his successor on the throne — a sign of the covenant of 2 Samuel 7 beginning to be fulfilled.

f.w: which hath given one to sit on my throne this day

chapters.n: Adonijah’s guests panic and scatter.
Adonijah, terrified of Solomon, runs to the altar and grabs its horns, seeking sanctuary.

f.w: caught hold on the horns of the altar
f.g: Horn-like projections on the altar’s corners; grasping them was a plea for protection.

chapters.n: Solomon is told that Adonijah refuses to let go until Solomon swears not to kill him.
Solomon promises mercy on one condition: if Adonijah proves loyal, not a hair of his head will be harmed; but if he does wrong, he will die.

f.w: there shall not an hair of him fall to the earth

chapters.n: Adonijah is brought down from the altar and bows before King Solomon, acknowledging his rule. Solomon sends him home — a merciful but watchful beginning.

f.g: Go home — you are spared, but kept away from power.

chapters.n: As death approaches, David gives Solomon his final charge — a father’s last instructions to a son who must now lead God’s people.

f.g: Gave solemn instructions.

chapters.n: “I go the way of all the earth” — David speaks calmly of his death. He urges Solomon to be strong and act with maturity and courage.

f.w: I go the way of all the earth

chapters.n: The heart of David’s charge: obey God’s law as given through Moses, and you will prosper. True success flows from faithfulness.

f.w: keep the charge of the LORD thy God

f.g: God’s solemn witnesses or covenant declarations.

chapters.n: David reminds Solomon that God’s promise of a lasting dynasty depends on his descendants walking faithfully before God with all their heart and soul.

f.w: with all their heart and with all their soul

chapters.n: David turns to unfinished business. Joab murdered two commanders, Abner and Amasa, in peacetime as if in war, staining himself — and David’s reign — with innocent blood.

f.w: shed the blood of war in peace
f.g: Killed men in peacetime as though it were battle — murder.

chapters.n: David asks Solomon to use his wisdom so that Joab doesn’t die peacefully in old age. Unpunished bloodshed was believed to defile the land and the king’s house.

f.g: Gray head — old age.

chapters.n: In contrast, Barzillai’s sons are to be honored with a place at the king’s table, in gratitude for their father’s loyalty during Absalom’s revolt.
David brings up Shimei, who cursed him bitterly. David had sworn not to kill him personally.

f.g: Severe, terrible.

chapters.n: But David’s oath does not bind Solomon. Using his wisdom, Solomon is to deal with Shimei’s guilt. A curse against the Lord’s anointed was a serious crime under the law.
David dies and is buried in the City of David. Peter mentions his tomb as still known in Jesus’ day.
David reigned forty years: seven in Hebron and thirty-three in Jerusalem.
Solomon takes David’s throne, and his kingdom is firmly established — a theme this chapter repeats.
Adonijah approaches Bath-sheba, Solomon’s mother. Wary, she asks if he comes in peace.
He says he has something to ask of her.
Adonijah claims the kingdom should have been his and that all Israel expected him to reign — an exaggeration — but admits the Lord gave it to Solomon.

f.w: it was his from the LORD

chapters.n: He has one request and asks her not to refuse.

f.g: Request.

chapters.n: He asks her to request Abishag, David’s nurse, as his wife. Bath-sheba may not see the danger, but marrying a king’s companion could be read as a claim to his throne.
Bath-sheba agrees to speak to the king for him.
Solomon honors his mother: he rises, bows, and seats her on a throne at his right hand. In Israel, the king’s mother held a position of great dignity.

f.g: The queen mother (gebirah) was an influential figure in Judah’s royal court.
The place of highest honor.

chapters.n: She calls it a small request, and Solomon promises not to refuse her.
She asks that Abishag be given to Adonijah as his wife.
Solomon immediately sees through it: why not ask for the kingdom itself for his older brother and his supporters, Abiathar and Joab? He views it as a renewed bid for the throne.

f.w: ask for him the kingdom also

chapters.n: Solomon swears a solemn oath that Adonijah’s request will cost him his life.

f.w: God do so to me, and more also
f.g: A standard oath: may God punish me severely if I don’t carry this out.

chapters.n: Solomon cites God’s faithfulness in establishing him as king and building him a “house” — a dynasty — as promised. He orders Adonijah’s execution.

f.w: who hath made me an house, as he promised

chapters.n: Benaiah carries out the sentence. Adonijah had been warned that any further disloyalty would mean death.

f.g: Attacked and killed him.

chapters.n: Abiathar, who supported Adonijah, deserves death, but Solomon spares him because he carried the ark and suffered alongside David. He is banished to his estate in Anathoth.

f.g: A priestly town in Benjamin, a few miles northeast of Jerusalem; later Jeremiah’s hometown.

f.w: afflicted in all wherein my father was afflicted

chapters.n: Removing Abiathar from the priesthood fulfills the prophecy against the house of Eli, from which Abiathar descended. God’s word, spoken about a century before, comes to pass.

f.w: the word of the LORD, which he spake concerning the house of Eli

chapters.n: Joab hears the news and flees to the tabernacle, grabbing the horns of the altar for sanctuary. He had stayed loyal through Absalom’s revolt but backed Adonijah.

f.w: caught hold on the horns of the altar

chapters.n: Solomon is told where Joab is and sends Benaiah to execute him.
Joab refuses to leave the altar, saying he will die there. Benaiah reports back to the king.
Solomon orders Benaiah to do as Joab said. The law gave no sanctuary at the altar to a deliberate murderer, and removing Joab cleanses David’s house from bloodguilt.
Joab’s guilt returns on his own head: he killed two men more righteous than himself without David’s knowledge.

f.w: my father David not knowing thereof

chapters.n: The guilt for their blood rests on Joab’s line, but Solomon prays that David’s house and throne will have the Lord’s peace forever.

f.w: peace for ever from the LORD

chapters.n: Benaiah kills Joab, and he is buried at his family property in the wilderness of Judah.

f.g: Buried on his own estate.

chapters.n: Solomon promotes Benaiah to army commander and makes Zadok the leading priest. Zadok’s family would hold the high priesthood for generations.

f.g: In his place.

chapters.n: Solomon puts Shimei under a kind of house arrest: he must live in Jerusalem and never leave.

f.w: go not forth thence any whither
f.g: Do not go anywhere outside the city.

chapters.n: If Shimei crosses the Kidron Valley — the road toward his home in Bahurim — he will die, and it will be his own fault.

f.w: thy blood shall be upon thine own head

chapters.n: Shimei agrees the terms are fair and lives in Jerusalem for a long time.
Three years later, two of Shimei’s slaves run away to Achish, king of Gath.
Shimei saddles his donkey, goes to Gath, and brings them back — ignoring his oath.
Solomon learns that Shimei left Jerusalem and returned.
Solomon reminds him that he swore by the Lord to stay, and agreed the terms were good.

f.g: Protested = solemnly warned.

chapters.n: Why did he break his oath before the Lord and the king’s command?
Solomon reminds Shimei of the evil he did to David. Now the Lord is bringing his wickedness back on his own head.

f.g: Aware of, sharing in the secret of.

chapters.n: But Solomon himself will be blessed, and David’s throne established forever before the Lord.

f.w: the throne of David shall be established before the LORD for ever

chapters.n: Benaiah executes Shimei. The chapter closes with its theme: the kingdom is now firmly established in Solomon’s hand. The violent loose ends of David’s reign have been resolved.

f.w: the kingdom was established in the hand of Solomon

chapters.n: Solomon seals a political alliance with Egypt by marrying Pharaoh’s daughter — a sign of Israel’s new international importance. But marrying foreign wives would later turn his heart; the Joseph Smith Translation adds that the Lord was not pleased with this marriage.

f.g: Formed an alliance by marriage. JST: “And the Lord was not pleased with Solomon, for he made affinity with Pharaoh.”

chapters.n: Because there was no temple yet, the people worshipped at “high places” — hilltop shrines. These were tolerated for a time but later became centers of idolatry.

f.g: Hilltop or elevated sites of worship, often with an altar.

f.w: there was no house built unto the name of the LORD

chapters.n: Solomon loved the Lord and followed David’s example — with one reservation: he also worshipped at the high places. The word “only” hints at a crack that will later widen.

f.g: A quiet qualification — his devotion was real but not yet complete.

chapters.n: Solomon goes to Gibeon, the most important high place because the tabernacle of Moses was there, and offers a thousand burnt offerings.

f.g: A lavish act of worship, perhaps over several days.

chapters.n: That night the Lord appears to Solomon in a dream with an open invitation: “Ask what I shall give thee.” What we ask for reveals what we truly value.

f.w: the LORD appeared to Solomon in a dream
Ask what I shall give thee

chapters.n: Solomon begins with gratitude, praising God’s loyal love to David, who walked faithfully, and for placing David’s son on the throne.

f.g: Hebrew ḥesed — steadfast, covenant love.

chapters.n: He humbly admits he feels like a little child, unsure how to lead. Recognizing one’s own inadequacy is the beginning of real wisdom.

f.w: I am but a little child
how to go out or come in
f.g: How to lead, especially in daily affairs and in war.

chapters.n: He feels the weight of leading God’s chosen people, too numerous to count.
His request: an “understanding heart” — literally a “hearing heart” — so he can judge rightly and tell good from evil. It is a model prayer for anyone with responsibility.

f.g: Hebrew lev shomea — a listening, obedient heart.

f.w: that I may discern between good and bad

chapters.n: The Lord is pleased with Solomon’s request.
God notes what Solomon did not ask for — long life, wealth, or victory over enemies — but wisdom to govern justly.

f.g: To understand what is just and to make fair decisions.

chapters.n: God grants him a wise and discerning heart beyond anyone before or after him.

f.w: a wise and an understanding heart

chapters.n: God also gives what he did not ask for — riches and honor greater than any other king. Seeking first what matters most brings other blessings too.

f.w: that which thou hast not asked

chapters.n: But one blessing is conditional: if Solomon walks in God’s ways as David did, God will lengthen his life.

f.w: if thou wilt walk in my ways

chapters.n: Solomon wakes and realizes it was a revelatory dream. He goes to Jerusalem, worships before the ark, and holds a feast for his servants.

f.g: Offerings shared in a fellowship meal with God and others.

chapters.n: Now comes a test of the gift. Two prostitutes — women of the lowest status — come to the king for judgment. Even they could appeal directly to the king.

f.g: Prostitutes.

chapters.n: The first woman explains that both women live in the same house and she gave birth there.

f.w: I was delivered of a child
f.g: I gave birth.

chapters.n: Three days later the other woman also gave birth. No one else was in the house — so there are no witnesses.

f.g: No one else; no outsider who could testify.

chapters.n: The other woman’s baby died in the night because she rolled over on it while sleeping.

f.g: She lay on it and smothered it.

chapters.n: The first woman claims the other secretly swapped the babies while she slept.

f.g: Arms or lap — close beside her.

chapters.n: In the morning she found a dead baby beside her, but looking closely, she knew it was not hers.

f.g: To nurse my baby.

chapters.n: The second woman denies everything, and they argue back and forth before the king. It is one word against another.
Solomon summarizes the stalemate: each claims the living child.

f.g: Solomon carefully restates both claims, showing he has listened.

chapters.n: Then he calls for a sword.

f.g: A shocking order meant to reveal the women’s hearts.

chapters.n: He orders the living baby cut in two and divided between them — a test designed to reveal true love.

f.w: Divide the living child in two

chapters.n: The real mother, moved with love, begs the king to give the baby to the other woman rather than kill him. The other woman says to divide him. True love would rather lose than see the child harmed.

f.w: her bowels yearned upon her son
f.g: Her deepest compassion was stirred; the Hebrew word is related to “womb.”
In no way; by no means.

chapters.n: Solomon declares that the woman who wanted the child to live is the mother. Wisdom saw through to the heart.
All Israel hears of the judgment and stands in awe, recognizing that God’s wisdom was in their king. The dream at Gibeon has been confirmed in action.

f.w: the wisdom of God was in him

f.g: Here, held in reverent respect.

chapters.n: This chapter describes how Solomon organized his kingdom. It opens with a simple but significant statement: he ruled over all Israel, a united nation.
A list of Solomon’s chief officials begins. Azariah, a grandson of Zadok, serves as a priest — showing how the Zadok family now led the priesthood.

f.g: Chief officials, cabinet members.
“Son” here may mean grandson; Zadok’s son was Ahimaaz.

chapters.n: Two brothers serve as royal secretaries, and Jehoshaphat continues as recorder from David’s administration — a sign of continuity.

f.g: Royal secretaries handling official documents.

chapters.n: Benaiah commands the army. Abiathar is still listed among the priests, perhaps in title only, since Solomon had banished him.
Two sons of Nathan — perhaps the prophet — hold high positions: one over the district governors, the other as the king’s personal adviser.

f.g: An official title for a trusted royal counselor.

chapters.n: Ahishar manages the palace, and Adoniram oversees forced labor — a growing burden that will later fuel the northern tribes’ revolt.

f.g: Palace manager or chief steward.

f.w: Adoniram the son of Abda was over the tribute
f.g: Tribute here means forced labor (Hebrew mas).

chapters.n: Solomon divides Israel into twelve districts, each with a governor responsible for supplying the royal court for one month a year.

f.g: Food, provisions.
The districts did not follow tribal boundaries exactly, perhaps to strengthen central control.

chapters.n: The list of governors begins. The first oversees the hill country of Ephraim, the heart of the northern tribes.

f.g: Some governors are listed only by their fathers’ names, perhaps because the original record was damaged or used family titles.

chapters.n: The second district covers towns in the old territory of Dan, west of Jerusalem.
The third covers land in the Sharon plain, along the coast.
The fourth covers the coastal region around Dor. This governor married one of Solomon’s daughters, binding him closely to the king.

f.g: A port city on the Mediterranean coast south of Mount Carmel.

chapters.n: The fifth covers the fertile Jezreel Valley and its fortress cities, from Megiddo to the Jordan.

f.g: A strategic fortress city guarding a key pass; later associated with Armageddon (Revelation 16:16).

chapters.n: The sixth governs northern Gilead east of the Jordan, including sixty walled cities with bronze gate bars.

f.g: A region in Bashan, east of the Sea of Galilee.
Sixty.

chapters.n: The seventh is based at Mahanaim, the city where David had taken refuge from Absalom.
The eighth, over Naphtali in Galilee, is Ahimaaz — possibly the loyal runner of David’s day — who married another of Solomon’s daughters.
The ninth is over Asher in the northwest; his father may be Hushai, David’s loyal friend.
The tenth governs Issachar, the fertile land around the Jezreel Valley.
The eleventh is over Benjamin, Saul’s old tribe.
The twelfth covers southern Gilead, the former kingdoms of Sihon and Og conquered in Moses’ day.

f.w: Sihon king of the Amorites, and of Og king of Bashan
the only officer which was in the land
f.g: Possibly meaning there was one more governor over Judah, which is not otherwise listed.

chapters.n: Under Solomon, Israel is numerous and prosperous, enjoying peace and plenty — a partial fulfillment of God’s promise to Abraham.

f.w: as the sand which is by the sea

chapters.n: Solomon’s rule extends from the Euphrates to Philistia and the border of Egypt — the boundaries God promised Abraham. Neighboring kingdoms pay him tribute.

f.w: from the river unto the land of the Philistines

f.g: The Euphrates.

chapters.n: The daily food for Solomon’s court was enormous — about 150 bushels of fine flour and twice as much coarser meal.

f.g: Hebrew kor, a large dry measure, perhaps about 6.5 bushels (220 liters).

chapters.n: Add to that dozens of cattle, a hundred sheep, and various game and poultry each day. The court must have fed thousands.

f.g: Different kinds of deer and gazelle.
Fattened birds, perhaps geese or poultry.

chapters.n: Solomon controlled all the land west of the Euphrates, from Tiphsah to Gaza, and had peace on every side. His name, related to shalom, fits his reign.

f.g: A crossing on the Euphrates in northern Syria.
Gaza, on the southwest coast.

f.w: he had peace on all sides

chapters.n: Everyone lived safely “under his vine and under his fig tree” — a beloved image of peace and security that the prophets later used for the Messiah’s reign.

f.w: every man under his vine and under his fig tree

chapters.n: Solomon built a large chariot force. Some numbers differ in Chronicles. The law warned kings against multiplying horses, a warning Solomon would ignore.

f.g: Chronicles says four thousand, likely the more original number.

chapters.n: The district governors supplied everything the royal table needed, each in his assigned month. Nothing was lacking.

f.g: The system worked efficiently, though it placed heavy demands on the people.

chapters.n: They also delivered barley and straw for the horses and swift steeds wherever they were stationed.

f.g: Here probably swift horses or chariot steeds, not camels.

chapters.n: God gave Solomon exceptional wisdom, understanding, and breadth of mind — as vast as the sand on the seashore.

f.g: Breadth of understanding — a mind that could grasp a great range of subjects.

chapters.n: His wisdom surpassed that of the famous wise men of the East and of Egypt, two centers of ancient learning.

f.w: the children of the east country
f.g: Peoples east of Israel, such as the Arabians and Mesopotamians, known for proverbs and riddles (compare Job 1:3).

chapters.n: He was wiser than renowned sages of his day. Ethan and Heman are linked to the titles of Psalms 88 and 89.
Solomon composed three thousand proverbs and over a thousand songs. Some of his sayings are preserved in the book of Proverbs, and Psalms 72 and 127 bear his name.
His knowledge reached into nature — from the great cedars of Lebanon to the small hyssop growing from a wall, and to animals, birds, reptiles, and fish.

f.w: the cedar tree that is in Lebanon

f.g: A small, bushy plant used in purification rituals.

chapters.n: People came from every nation, sent by kings who had heard of his wisdom — like the Queen of Sheba later. Jesus would say that “a greater than Solomon is here.”

f.w: there came of all people to hear the wisdom of Solomon

chapters.n: Hiram, king of the Phoenician city of Tyre, sends envoys to congratulate Solomon. He had been a long-time friend and ally of David.

f.g: A loyal ally; “love” was treaty language for faithful friendship between kings.

chapters.n: Solomon responds with a proposal of his own.
He explains that David could not build the temple because of constant wars. Chronicles adds that David had shed much blood, so God reserved the task for a man of peace.

f.w: under the soles of his feet
f.g: Completely subdued, an image of total victory.

chapters.n: Now God has given Solomon peace on every side, with no enemy or disaster to distract him. Peace is the right setting for building a house of God.

f.g: Misfortune or disaster that occurs.

chapters.n: Solomon announces his plan to build a temple for the Lord’s name, fulfilling God’s promise to David that his son would do so.

f.w: an house unto the name of the LORD
f.g: God’s “name” stands for His presence, authority, and character.

f.w: he shall build an house unto my name

chapters.n: He asks Hiram to have cedars cut in Lebanon, offering to pay the workers. The Phoenicians were the ancient world’s finest timber craftsmen.

f.g: The cedars of Lebanon were prized for their size, durability, and fragrance.
Know how to cut.
Phoenicians; Sidon and Tyre were their main cities.

chapters.n: Hiram rejoices and praises the Lord for giving David such a wise son. Even this foreign king recognizes Israel’s God and Solomon’s wisdom.

f.w: Blessed be the LORD this day

chapters.n: Hiram agrees to supply all the cedar and fir (or cypress) timber Solomon wants.

f.g: Probably juniper or cypress.

chapters.n: His men will haul the logs to the coast, tie them into rafts, and float them south to Solomon’s chosen port. In exchange Hiram asks for food for his household.

f.g: Rafts of logs.

f.w: the place that thou shalt appoint
f.g: Chronicles names Joppa, the port nearest Jerusalem.

chapters.n: Hiram provides all the cedar and cypress Solomon needs.
Solomon pays with large annual shipments of wheat and pressed olive oil. Phoenicia, a narrow coastal land, depended on Israel’s farmland for food.

f.g: Measures = kors; a very large amount of grain.
The finest beaten olive oil.

chapters.n: God keeps His promise of wisdom, seen in the peace and treaty Solomon forms with Hiram.

f.g: A covenant, a formal treaty.

chapters.n: Solomon drafts thirty thousand Israelite men into forced labor for the project.

f.g: A labor draft; conscripted workers.

chapters.n: They work in rotating shifts — one month in Lebanon, two months home — under Adoniram’s supervision. Still, this burden would later cause resentment.

f.g: In rotating shifts.

chapters.n: Seventy thousand carriers and eighty thousand stonecutters work in the hills. Chronicles indicates many were non-Israelite residents of the land.

f.g: Stonecutters in the quarries.

chapters.n: Thirty-three hundred foremen supervise the workers.

f.g: Chronicles gives 3,600, perhaps counting differently.

chapters.n: Large, costly, carefully dressed stones are quarried for the temple’s foundation. The house of the Lord was to rest on the finest foundation.
Israelite and Phoenician craftsmen, including masons from Gebal, work together to prepare timber and stone. Israelites and foreigners join in building God’s house.

f.g: Hebrew Giblim — men of Gebal (Byblos), a Phoenician city famous for stonework.

chapters.n: Construction of the temple begins in Solomon’s fourth year, about 480 years after the Exodus. The date links the temple to Israel’s deliverance from Egypt: freedom led to a house where God could dwell among His people.

f.w: the four hundred and eightieth year
f.g: Possibly a symbolic number (12 generations of 40 years) or an exact count; scholars differ on dating the Exodus.
Ziv, the second month of the year, in April–May — “the month of brightness” or flowers.

chapters.n: The main building is about 90 feet long, 30 feet wide, and 45 feet high — not huge by modern standards, but magnificent in materials and meaning. It doubles the tabernacle’s dimensions.

60 cubits.

chapters.n: A porch, or entrance hall, extends across the front of the building.

chapters.n: High, narrow windows let in light — probably latticed openings near the top of the walls.

f.g: Possibly windows with recessed frames, or latticed openings.

chapters.n: Rooms are built in stories along the outside walls of the main hall and the inner sanctuary — likely storerooms for temple supplies and treasures.

f.g: Hebrew devir — the innermost room, the Holy of Holies, where God “spoke.”
Side rooms, arranged in three stories.

Ledges or offsets in the wall.

chapters.n: The stones were cut and finished at the quarry, so no hammer, axe, or iron tool was heard at the temple site. The house of God rose in reverent quiet. Many see a lesson here: God shapes His people in the world so they can fit peacefully into His holy house.

f.w: neither hammer nor axe nor any tool of iron

chapters.n: The entrance to the side rooms is on the south side, with a winding staircase or ladder leading to the upper floors.

f.g: The south side, if facing east toward the entrance.
Possibly a spiral staircase, or trapdoors and ladders.

chapters.n: Solomon completes the structure and roofs it with cedar beams and planks.

f.g: Roofed.

chapters.n: The side rooms, each story about 7.5 feet high, are attached to the temple with cedar beams.
In the midst of the construction, the word of the Lord comes to Solomon.

f.w: the word of the LORD came to Solomon
f.g: Perhaps through a prophet, or by direct revelation.

chapters.n: God reminds him that the building alone is not enough. If Solomon keeps His commandments, God will fulfill His promises to David. The temple’s value depends on the faithfulness of the people.

f.w: if thou wilt walk in my statutes

chapters.n: Then God will dwell among Israel and never forsake His people — the true purpose of any temple.

f.w: I will dwell among the children of Israel

chapters.n: Solomon finishes building the house — the narrator repeats it for emphasis.

chapters.n: At the back, a cedar partition walls off a 30-foot section to form the inner sanctuary, the Most Holy Place.

The second cherub has the same size and shape as the first — perfect symmetry.
Both stand 15 feet tall.
The cherubim stand side by side; their outer wings touch the side walls and their inner wings meet in the middle. The ark would rest beneath their outstretched wings, as if under God’s throne.
The cherubim are overlaid with gold.
All the walls are carved with cherubim, palm trees, and open flowers — angels and garden imagery suggesting a return to the presence of God, as in Eden.
Even the floor of both rooms is overlaid with gold.

f.g: In the inner sanctuary and the outer room.

chapters.n: The entrance to the inner sanctuary has doors of olive wood with a five-sided doorframe.

f.w: a fifth part of the wall
f.g: The Hebrew may mean a five-sided or pentagonal frame.

chapters.n: The olive-wood doors are carved with cherubim, palms, and flowers, all overlaid with gold.
The main entrance has doorposts of olive wood with a four-sided frame.

f.w: a fourth part of the wall
f.g: Possibly a four-sided (rectangular) frame.

chapters.n: Its two doors are of cypress, each made of two folding panels.

f.g: Panels of a door.

chapters.n: They too are carved with cherubim, palms, and flowers and overlaid with fitted gold.

f.g: The priests’ court around the temple, where the altar of sacrifice stood.

chapters.n: The foundation was laid in Solomon’s fourth year, in the month of Ziv.
The temple is finished seven years later, in the month of Bul, in every detail. Seven years — the number of completeness — fits the building of God’s house.

f.g: The eighth month, October–November, the time of autumn rains.
About seven and a half years by exact count; seven also echoes the seven days of creation.

chapters.n: Solomon spends thirteen years building his own palace complex — almost twice as long as the seven years spent on the temple. The contrast may quietly hint at shifting priorities.
The “House of the Forest of Lebanon,” about 150 by 75 feet, was named for its many cedar pillars, which made the hall feel like a forest. It served as a royal hall and armory.

f.w: the house of the forest of Lebanon

chapters.n: Its cedar roof rested on forty-five beams or pillars, arranged fifteen to a row.
Windows were set in three rows, facing each other across the hall.

f.g: Window opposite window.

chapters.n: Its doorways and frames were rectangular, with windows facing each other in three tiers.

f.g: Rectangular frames.

chapters.n: He also built a colonnade, or Hall of Pillars, about 75 by 45 feet, with a porch and canopy in front.

f.g: A colonnaded hall or portico.

chapters.n: He built the Hall of Judgment, where his throne stood and he decided cases — the place where wisdom like that shown in chapter 3 would be exercised. It was paneled in cedar.
His private residence stood in another courtyard behind the hall. He also built a similar palace for his Egyptian wife, Pharaoh’s daughter.
All these buildings used expensive cut stone, sawn to measure and finished inside and out, from foundation to top.

f.g: The top course of a wall.

chapters.n: The foundations were enormous blocks, some 12 to 15 feet long.

f.g: About 15 feet (4.5 m).

chapters.n: Above the foundations were more fine cut stones and cedar beams.
The great courtyard, like the temple’s inner court, was walled with three rows of cut stone and a row of cedar beams.

f.w: three rows of hewed stones, and a row of cedar beams

chapters.n: For the temple’s bronze work, Solomon brings a master craftsman named Hiram (also called Huram) from Tyre — not the king of the same name.
Hiram’s mother was an Israelite widow and his father a Tyrian bronze worker. Like Bezaleel, who built the tabernacle, he was filled with wisdom and skill for sacred work.

f.w: a widow's son of the tribe of Naphtali
f.g: Chronicles says his mother was from Dan; she may have been of Dan by birth and married into Naphtali, or the reverse.
Skill, craftsmanship.

chapters.n: He casts two great bronze pillars, each about 27 feet tall and 18 feet around.

f.g: Bronze.

chapters.n: Each pillar is topped with a cast bronze capital about 7.5 feet high.

f.g: Capitals — the decorative tops of columns.

chapters.n: The capitals are decorated with lattice networks and chain-like wreaths, seven on each.

f.g: Lattice or net-patterned decoration.

chapters.n: Two rows of bronze pomegranates encircle each capital over the latticework.

f.g: Pomegranates, full of seeds, symbolized fruitfulness and also decorated the high priest’s robe.

chapters.n: The upper parts of the capitals in the porch are shaped like lilies, about 6 feet high.

f.g: Lily or lotus designs — symbols of life and beauty.

chapters.n: Two hundred pomegranates in rows circle each capital, above the rounded bulge next to the latticework.

f.g: The rounded, bowl-shaped part of the capital.

chapters.n: The pillars stand at the temple entrance and receive names: Jachin (“He will establish”) and Boaz (“In Him is strength”). Together they proclaim that God establishes His house and gives it strength.

f.g: “He (God) will establish.”
“In Him is strength” — also the name of David’s ancestor (Ruth 4:21).

chapters.n: With the lily designs on top, the pillars are finished.
Hiram casts a huge round bronze basin, the “molten sea,” 15 feet across and 7.5 feet high. The priests used it for washing.

f.g: A massive cast-metal basin; Chronicles says it was for the priests to wash in.
A rounded figure for the circumference.

chapters.n: Two rows of gourd-shaped ornaments, cast in one piece with the basin, run around it under the rim.

f.g: Gourd-shaped knobs; Chronicles describes them as oxen-like figures.

chapters.n: The sea rests on twelve bronze oxen, three facing each direction — perhaps representing the twelve tribes. Baptismal fonts in Latter-day Saint temples follow this pattern, resting on twelve oxen.

f.g: Hindquarters.

chapters.n: The basin’s walls are a handbreadth thick, its rim flared like a cup or lily blossom. It held around 11,000 gallons.

f.g: About 3 inches (7.5 cm).
A bath was about 5.8 gallons (22 liters); 2 Chronicles 4:5 gives 3,000.

chapters.n: Hiram also makes ten bronze carts or stands, each about 6 feet square and 4.5 feet high, to carry water basins.

f.g: Movable stands on wheels.

chapters.n: The stands are built with panels set between frames.

f.g: Panels.
Frames or crossbars.

chapters.n: The panels are decorated with lions, oxen, and cherubim, with hanging wreaths or garlands below.

f.g: Garlands or wreaths of hammered metal.

chapters.n: Each stand has four bronze wheels and axles, with supports at the corners to hold the basin.

f.g: Supports or brackets.

chapters.n: The opening on top of each stand, made to hold a basin, is round, with square-paneled engravings around it.

f.g: Engravings.

chapters.n: The wheels, about 27 inches high, are under the panels, with axles attached to the stand.
They are built like chariot wheels — axles, hubs, rims, and spokes, all cast in bronze.

f.g: Hubs.
Rims of a wheel.

chapters.n: Each stand has four corner supports cast as part of the stand itself.
A round band about 9 inches high runs around the top, with supports and panels cast in one piece.

f.g: A circular band or rim.

chapters.n: Cherubim, lions, and palm trees are engraved wherever there is space, surrounded by wreaths.

f.g: Uniform craftsmanship — order and harmony in God’s house.

chapters.n: Ten bronze basins, each holding about 230 gallons, sit on the stands. Chronicles says they were used to rinse the parts of burnt offerings.

f.g: Washing basins.
About 230 gallons (880 liters).

chapters.n: Five stands are placed on each side of the temple, and the great sea at the southeast corner.

f.g: The south side.

chapters.n: Hiram also makes the smaller items — basins, shovels for ashes, and sprinkling bowls — completing his work for the temple.

f.g: Used to remove ashes from the altar.
Sprinkling bowls for sacrificial blood.

chapters.n: A summary of Hiram’s work begins: the two pillars with their bowl-shaped capitals and the latticework covering them.
The four hundred pomegranates — two rows for each lattice on the capitals.
The ten stands and their ten basins.
The great sea and the twelve oxen beneath it.
All the pots, shovels, and bowls, made of burnished bronze.

f.g: Polished bronze.

chapters.n: These items were cast in clay molds in the Jordan Valley, where the clay soil was ideal for metal casting.

f.g: Towns in the Jordan Valley; archaeologists have found evidence of ancient metalworking in this region.

chapters.n: There was so much bronze that it was never weighed — the amount could not be calculated.

f.w: neither was the weight of the brass found out

chapters.n: Solomon also made the golden furnishings for inside the temple: the golden incense altar and the table for the bread of the Presence.

f.g: Bread of the Presence — twelve loaves set before the Lord continually.

chapters.n: Ten lampstands of pure gold stood before the inner sanctuary, five on each side, with golden flower decorations, lamps, and tongs.

f.g: Lampstands (oil lamps, not candles).
Used to trim lamp wicks.

chapters.n: Even the smallest tools — bowls, wick trimmers, basins, ladles, firepans — and the door hinges for both rooms were made of gold. Nothing in God’s house was too small to matter.

f.g: Wick trimmers.
Firepans for carrying coals and burning incense.
Namely, that is.

chapters.n: The work is complete. Solomon brings in the silver, gold, and articles David had dedicated and stores them in the temple treasury, honoring his father’s preparations.

f.w: the things which David his father had dedicated

chapters.n: With the temple finished, Solomon gathers Israel’s leaders to bring the ark of the covenant from David’s tent in the City of David up to the new temple on the higher hill.

f.w: the ark of the covenant of the LORD

f.g: Here the original City of David, just south of the temple mount.

chapters.n: All Israel assembles during the great autumn festival in the seventh month — the Feast of Tabernacles, which celebrated God’s care in the wilderness.

f.g: The Feast of Tabernacles (Booths).
The seventh month (September–October), later called Tishri.

chapters.n: The elders arrive, and the priests lift the ark — this time carried properly, as the law required.

f.w: the priests took up the ark

chapters.n: The priests and Levites bring up the ark, along with the old tabernacle of Moses and its sacred vessels, which were now stored in the temple.

f.g: The tent of meeting from Moses’ day, which had been at Gibeon.

chapters.n: Solomon and the people offer countless sacrifices as the ark proceeds — an outpouring of worship.

f.w: could not be told nor numbered
f.g: Too many to count.

chapters.n: The priests place the ark in the Most Holy Place, under the wings of the great cherubim.

f.w: under the wings of the cherubims

chapters.n: The cherubim’s outstretched wings overshadow the ark and its carrying poles.

f.g: Carrying poles.

chapters.n: Inside the ark were only the two stone tablets of the covenant that Moses placed there at Sinai (Horeb).

f.g: Another name for Mount Sinai.

chapters.n: As the priests leave, a cloud fills the temple — the same visible sign of God’s presence that filled the tabernacle in Moses’ day.

f.w: the cloud filled the house of the LORD

chapters.n: The glory of the Lord is so overwhelming that the priests cannot continue their service. God has accepted His house.
Solomon speaks: the Lord said He would dwell in thick darkness — the cloud that both reveals and veils His presence.
He declares he has built a lofty house for God, a settled dwelling place forever.

f.w: a settled place for thee to abide in for ever

chapters.n: Solomon turns to face the standing congregation and blesses them.
He praises God, who promised David with His mouth and fulfilled it with His hand — God’s word and deed always match.
Since the Exodus, God had not chosen a city for His house; instead He chose David to lead His people.
Building a temple had been David’s heart’s desire.

f.w: it was in the heart of David

chapters.n: God commended David for that desire, even though He did not let him build it. God honors righteous desires of the heart.

f.w: thou didst well that it was in thine heart

chapters.n: Instead, David’s son would build it.
God has kept His word: Solomon is king and the house is built.

f.w: the LORD hath performed his word

chapters.n: Solomon has made a place for the ark, which holds the covenant God made with Israel at the Exodus. The temple is a house of covenants.

f.w: wherein is the covenant of the LORD

chapters.n: Solomon stands before the altar, facing all Israel, and lifts his hands toward heaven to begin his great dedicatory prayer. Latter-day Saints may notice similar themes in the Kirtland Temple dedicatory prayer.

f.w: spread forth his hands toward heaven

chapters.n: He begins with praise: no God is like the Lord, who keeps covenant and steadfast love with those who walk before Him wholeheartedly.

f.w: there is no God like thee

f.g: Mercy = ḥesed, steadfast covenant love.

chapters.n: God has kept His promise to David — again, spoken by His mouth and fulfilled by His hand.
Solomon asks God to keep the rest of His promise: a descendant on David’s throne, provided his children walk faithfully.

f.w: There shall not fail thee a man

chapters.n: He asks God to confirm His word to David.

f.g: Confirmed, proven true.

chapters.n: A profound question: can God truly dwell on earth? Even the highest heavens cannot contain Him — how much less this building? The temple does not confine God; it is a place where heaven and earth meet.

f.w: the heaven and heaven of heavens cannot contain thee

chapters.n: Still, Solomon humbly asks God to listen to his prayer and plea today.

f.g: Humble, earnest request.

chapters.n: He asks that God’s eyes be open toward this house day and night, where His name dwells, and hear prayers offered toward it.
The key refrain of the prayer begins: “Hear thou in heaven… and forgive.” The temple is a place to seek forgiveness and reconciliation with God.

f.w: hear thou in heaven thy dwelling place
f.g: This phrase repeats throughout the prayer, stressing that God truly dwells in heaven.

chapters.n: First case: when someone is accused of wronging a neighbor and swears an oath of innocence at the altar.

f.w: an oath be laid upon him

chapters.n: Solomon asks God to judge justly — condemning the guilty and vindicating the innocent.

f.g: Declaring the innocent to be in the right.

chapters.n: Second case: when Israel is defeated in battle because of sin, but then repents and prays at the temple.

f.w: because they have sinned against thee

chapters.n: May God forgive and restore them to their land.

f.w: bring them again unto the land

chapters.n: Third case: drought caused by sin. If they pray, confess, and turn from sin, Solomon asks God to respond.

f.w: that thou teach them the good way

chapters.n: Fourth case: any disaster — famine, plague, crop disease, locusts, siege, or sickness.

Probably a stage of the locust.

chapters.n: When anyone, aware of “the plague of his own heart,” prays toward this house — the personal sense of sin and need — Solomon asks God to hear.

f.w: the plague of his own heart
f.g: One’s own inner sorrow or sin.

chapters.n: May God forgive and deal with each person according to their heart, which only He truly knows.

f.w: that all people of the earth may know thy name

chapters.n: Sixth case: when Israel goes to battle at God’s direction and prays toward Jerusalem and the temple.
May God hear and uphold their cause.

f.g: Defend them; give them justice.

chapters.n: If in captivity they come to their senses, repent, and confess their sins, Solomon asks God to listen.

f.w: pray unto thee toward their land
with all their heart, and with all their soul

May He forgive them and move their captors to show them compassion — as later happened under Cyrus of Persia.

chapters.n: For they are God’s own people, whom He rescued from Egypt, that furnace of suffering.

chapters.n: Solomon asks God to keep His eyes open and His ears attentive to all their prayers.

Solomon rises from kneeling before the altar with hands raised to heaven. A king kneeling before God shows where true authority lies.
He stands and blesses the whole congregation in a loud voice.
He praises God for giving Israel rest; not one of His good promises through Moses has failed.

f.w: there hath not failed one word of all his good promise

chapters.n: The ultimate goal: that all peoples of the earth will know that the Lord is God and there is no other.

f.w: that the LORD is God, and that there is none else

chapters.n: The king and all Israel offer sacrifices before the Lord.

f.w: dedicated the house of the LORD
f.g: Dedicated = consecrated, set apart for holy use.

chapters.n: Afterward Solomon sends the people home. They bless the king and leave joyful, grateful for all God’s goodness to David and to Israel. This is a high point of Israel’s history.
About twenty years into his reign, Solomon has completed both the temple and his own palace complex. The narrator pauses at this high point, just before the Lord speaks to him again.
This is Solomon’s second recorded revelation. The first came at Gibeon, where he asked for an understanding heart. Now the Lord answers the dedicatory prayer he offered in chapter 8.

chapters.n: If Solomon is faithful, the Lord will keep His promise to David that a descendant would always sit on Israel’s throne.

chapters.n: The warning now shifts to “ye”—plural. It covers Solomon and all his descendants: turning to other gods would break the covenant.

chapters.n: The narrative turns from revelation to administration. Seven years for the temple and thirteen for the palace make twenty years of building.

a diplomatic term for an allied king of equal rank.
