chapters.n: Abijam’s deeds are in Judah’s royal records. Chronicles adds a battle where he called on Israel to return to the Lord.

f.w: there was war between Abijam and Jeroboam

chapters.n: Abijam dies, and his son Asa becomes king.
Asa begins his reign about 911 BC, in Jeroboam’s twentieth year.
Asa reigns a long forty-one years. “Maachah” here is his grandmother, who kept the title of queen mother.

f.g: ‘mother’ here likely means grandmother, the reigning queen mother.

chapters.n: Asa is the first king of Judah after the division to be called righteous like David.
He launches a reform: removing shrine prostitutes and the idols his predecessors had set up.

f.g: cult prostitutes associated with fertility worship.
Hebrew gillulim, a contemptuous word, perhaps ‘dung-idols.’

chapters.n: Asa shows courage by removing his own grandmother from her powerful position and burning her Asherah image in the Kidron Valley. Faithfulness to God sometimes requires difficult family choices.

f.g: an ‘obscene image’ for Asherah, the Canaanite mother-goddess.
the valley just east of Jerusalem.

chapters.n: The local “high places” remained, likely shrines where people still worshiped the Lord improperly outside the temple. Still, Asa’s heart was loyal to the Lord.

f.g: local hilltop shrines, discouraged once the temple was built.

chapters.n: He restored dedicated treasure—silver, gold, and vessels—to the temple, refilling what Shishak had taken.
Asa faced constant conflict with Baasha, the new king of Israel.
Baasha fortified Ramah, just five miles north of Jerusalem, to blockade Judah and stop people from crossing over to the south.

f.g: a town in Benjamin on the main road north of Jerusalem.
allow.

chapters.n: Rather than seeking the Lord, Asa empties the temple and palace treasuries to bribe Ben-hadad of Damascus. Chronicles reports that a prophet rebuked him for trusting a foreign king instead of God.

f.g: ‘son of Hadad,’ a title used by several Aramean kings.

chapters.n: Asa appeals to an old alliance and asks Ben-hadad to break his treaty with Israel.

f.g: treaty, alliance.

chapters.n: Ben-hadad accepts the bribe and attacks Israel’s northern towns around the Sea of Galilee.

f.g: the area around the Sea of Galilee (Chinnereth).
the northern tribal territory west of Galilee.

chapters.n: With war on his northern border, Baasha abandons Ramah and pulls back to his capital, Tirzah.
Asa drafts every man in Judah to haul away Baasha’s building materials and uses them to fortify his own border towns of Geba and Mizpah.

f.g: no one was excused from the labor.
‘watchtower,’ a strategic town in Benjamin.

chapters.n: Asa’s achievements are recorded in Judah’s records. In old age he suffered a disease in his feet; Chronicles notes he sought physicians rather than the Lord.
Asa dies and his son Jehoshaphat, another righteous king, succeeds him.
The story returns north. Jeroboam’s son Nadab reigns only about two years.
Nadab continues his father’s calf worship.
Baasha, from the tribe of Issachar, assassinates Nadab while the army is besieging the Philistine town of Gibbethon. Israel’s throne becomes a prize seized by force.

f.g: plotted a coup.
a Philistine-controlled town west of Israel’s hill country.

chapters.n: Baasha kills Nadab and takes the throne.
Baasha wipes out Jeroboam’s entire family, fulfilling Ahijah’s prophecy. God used Baasha’s violence to accomplish the judgment, though Baasha himself was not righteous.

f.w: according unto the saying of the LORD

chapters.n: The cause, again, was the sin of Jeroboam that led all Israel astray.
Nadab’s acts are recorded in Israel’s chronicles.
The note about war between Asa and Baasha repeats verse 16, framing Baasha’s reign.
Baasha rules Israel from Tirzah for twenty-four years.

f.g: Israel’s capital until Omri built Samaria.

chapters.n: Though he destroyed Jeroboam’s family for its sin, Baasha commits the same sin himself.

f.w: walked in the way of Jeroboam

chapters.n: The prophet Jehu son of Hanani (not the later king Jehu) carries the Lord’s message against Baasha. His father Hanani was also a prophet who rebuked Asa.
The charge echoes Ahijah’s words to Jeroboam: God raised Baasha from nothing, yet he repeated Jeroboam’s sin and led the people astray.

f.g: from humble, insignificant beginnings.

chapters.n: Baasha’s dynasty will be swept away just as Jeroboam’s was.

f.g: descendants.

chapters.n: The same grim curse of unburied bodies that fell on Jeroboam’s house will fall on Baasha’s.
Baasha’s other deeds and military strength are in Israel’s royal annals.
Baasha dies and is buried in Tirzah; his son Elah succeeds him.
The narrator adds a second reason for judgment: Baasha was condemned not only for idolatry but also because he killed Jeroboam’s house. God used Baasha, but did not excuse his violent ambition.
Elah reigns only about two years, around 886–885 BC.
Zimri, a chariot commander, plots against Elah while the king is getting drunk at his steward’s house—an image of a careless ruler.

f.g: commander of one of two chariot divisions.

chapters.n: Zimri assassinates Elah and seizes the throne.
Zimri immediately kills all of Baasha’s male relatives and even his supporters, to eliminate any rival claim.

f.g: relatives, specifically avengers of blood (Hebrew go’alim).

chapters.n: This fulfills Jehu’s prophecy against Baasha.
Their sin was idolatry—“vanities,” worthless idols with no substance.

f.g: Hebrew hevel: vapor, emptiness; a scornful term for idols.

chapters.n: Elah’s deeds are recorded in Israel’s chronicles.
Zimri’s reign lasts just seven days. Meanwhile the army is again besieging Gibbethon.
Hearing of the coup, the army proclaims its own commander, Omri, as king on the spot.

f.g: founder of a powerful dynasty; Assyrian records later called Israel ‘the house of Omri.’

chapters.n: Omri marches on Tirzah and lays siege to it.
When the city falls, Zimri retreats into the palace citadel, sets it on fire, and dies in the flames.

f.g: the fortified inner citadel of the royal house.

chapters.n: His violent end is tied to his sins—he too followed Jeroboam’s ways.
Zimri’s treason is recorded in the royal annals. His name later became a byword for a traitor.
Israel splits into factions: half support Tibni, half support Omri. A brief civil war follows.
Omri’s side wins; Tibni dies, and Omri becomes sole king.
Omri reigns twelve years (about 885–874 BC), counting the years of rivalry with Tibni, six of them in Tirzah.
Omri buys a hill and builds a new capital, Samaria, named after its former owner Shemer. Its strong defensive position made it Israel’s capital until it fell to Assyria in 722 BC.

f.g: Hebrew Shomron, possibly linked to ‘watch’ or to Shemer.
about 150 pounds of silver.

chapters.n: Politically, Omri was strong; spiritually, he was worse than all before him.
He kept up Jeroboam’s calf worship and its empty idolatry.

f.g: worthless idols.

chapters.n: Kings says little about Omri’s accomplishments, which were considerable. Outside sources such as the Moabite Stone mention his conquest of Moab. The Bible’s interest is spiritual, not political.

f.g: his military power; see the Moabite (Mesha) Stone inscription.

chapters.n: Omri dies and is buried in Samaria; Ahab becomes king.
Ahab rules twenty-two years from Samaria (about 874–853 BC). His reign gets more space in Kings than any other northern king because of his clash with Elijah.
Ahab is judged the worst king yet.
Treating Jeroboam’s sins as trivial, Ahab marries Jezebel, a Phoenician princess, and actively worships Baal. This brings Canaanite Baal worship into Israel as a state religion.

f.g: Phoenician princess whose name honors Baal.
‘with Baal’; a priest-king of Tyre and Sidon.
‘lord’ or ‘master’; the Canaanite storm and fertility god believed to send rain.

chapters.n: He builds a temple to Baal in his own capital, complete with an altar.

f.g: set up, erected.

chapters.n: He also sets up an Asherah pole. More than any king before him, he provokes the Lord.

f.g: an Asherah, a wooden pole or image honoring the goddess Asherah.

chapters.n: A grim footnote: Hiel rebuilds Jericho, and his oldest and youngest sons die—fulfilling Joshua’s curse on anyone who rebuilt the city. It shows that God’s word endures across centuries, even in a time of rampant unbelief.

f.w: according to the word of the LORD, which he spake by Joshua

f.g: at the cost of his firstborn son’s life.

chapters.n: Elijah appears without introduction and confronts Ahab with a drought. His name means “my God is Jehovah”—a direct challenge to Baal, the supposed rain-god. Latter-day Saints honor Elijah as holding the sealing power, by which his word could bind the heavens.

f.g: Hebrew Eliyahu: ‘my God is Jehovah (the LORD).’
from Tishbe, a town in Gilead east of the Jordan.
whom I serve, as a servant stands ready before a king.

chapters.n: Immediately after Elijah’s declaration, the Lord gives him new direction.
He is sent into hiding east toward the Jordan, by a stream called Cherith—out of Ahab’s reach.

f.g: a seasonal stream (wadi), probably east of the Jordan; location uncertain.
east of, or facing, the Jordan.

chapters.n: God promises water from the brook and food from ravens—unclean birds under the law, now serving as God’s messengers of provision.

f.g: unclean birds under the law of Moses.

chapters.n: Elijah obeys exactly. His public boldness is matched by private trust and obedience.
Morning and evening the ravens bring bread and meat, recalling the manna and quail God gave Israel in the wilderness.

f.w: bread and flesh in the morning

chapters.n: Eventually the brook dries up. Elijah experiences the drought he announced, and must trust God for the next step.
Once again, the Lord’s word comes when needed.
God sends him to Zarephath, a Phoenician town near Sidon—Jezebel’s home territory and the heartland of Baal worship. There a widow, one of society’s poorest, will feed him.

f.g: a coastal town between Tyre and Sidon; in Greek, Sarepta.
provide food for.

chapters.n: At the town gate he meets a widow gathering sticks and asks for water—a precious thing in a drought.
As she goes, he also asks for a piece of bread, a far harder request.

f.g: a small piece.

chapters.n: She swears by “the LORD thy God,” recognizing Elijah as an Israelite. She has only enough flour and oil for one last meal before she and her son starve.

f.g: flour or ground grain.
a small jar or jug.
prepare it, cook it.

chapters.n: Elijah tells her not to fear, but to feed him first. It is a test of faith: give from her little before seeing the miracle.
He gives the Lord’s promise: her flour and oil will last until rain returns. Israel’s God provides in the land of Baal.

f.g: be used up, run out.

chapters.n: She obeys, and she, her son, and Elijah eat for many days.
The miracle continues day after day, exactly as promised. Many see it as a type of how the Lord blesses those who give in faith, as with the widow’s mite.

f.w: the barrel of meal wasted not

chapters.n: Later, her son becomes so ill that he stops breathing and dies.

f.g: severe.

chapters.n: In grief, she assumes that the presence of a holy man has exposed some past sin and brought punishment. Her question reflects a common ancient belief that suffering always comes from sin.

f.w: What have I to do with thee
f.g: an idiom meaning ‘Why are you involved with me?’ or ‘What have you against me?’

chapters.n: Elijah takes the boy from her arms to his upper room and lays him on his own bed.

f.g: an upper room or roof chamber.
arms, lap, embrace.

chapters.n: Elijah pours out his heart honestly to God, asking why such sorrow should fall on the woman who had sheltered him.

f.g: stay as a guest.

chapters.n: He stretches himself on the child three times and pleads for the boy’s life to return. This is the first recorded raising of the dead in the Bible.

f.g: Hebrew nephesh: life, breath, living being.

chapters.n: The Lord hears Elijah, and the boy comes back to life. God holds power over death itself—a foreshadowing of Christ’s raising of the widow’s son at Nain and His own resurrection.
Elijah brings the boy down and gives him back to his mother with simple words: “See, your son lives.”
The widow’s faith becomes certainty: Elijah is truly God’s prophet, and the Lord’s word through him is true. A Gentile woman confesses the God of Israel, while Israel itself serves Baal.
In the third year of drought the Lord sends Elijah back to face Ahab, with a promise that rain is coming. The New Testament gives the drought’s length as three and a half years.

f.g: present yourself, appear.

chapters.n: Elijah sets out. Samaria, the capital, is in the grip of severe famine.
Ahab summons Obadiah, the manager of his palace. The narrator notes that Obadiah (“servant of the LORD”) deeply revered the Lord, even serving in Ahab’s court.

f.g: ‘servant of Jehovah’; not the author of the book of Obadiah.
palace steward, a high royal official.

chapters.n: When Jezebel was killing the Lord’s prophets, Obadiah secretly hid a hundred of them in two caves and kept them alive. Faith can be quietly courageous inside a hostile system.

f.g: in groups of fifty, perhaps in two caves of Mount Carmel.

chapters.n: Ahab’s concern is for his horses and mules—vital for his chariot army—more than for his starving people.

f.g: perhaps.

chapters.n: The king and his steward split up to search the land for grazing.
Elijah meets Obadiah, who recognizes him and bows with deep respect.

f.w: Art thou that my lord Elijah?
f.g: ‘Is it you, my lord Elijah?’

chapters.n: Elijah tells Obadiah to announce to Ahab that he is here. Note the words “thy lord”: Obadiah serves Ahab, but Elijah serves the Lord.
Obadiah is terrified: delivering such a message could cost him his life.
Ahab had searched every neighboring kingdom for Elijah, even making rulers swear he was not hiding there.
Obadiah repeats the request in disbelief.
He fears the Spirit will whisk Elijah away, leaving Obadiah to face Ahab’s wrath. He reminds Elijah that he has been faithful to the Lord since youth.

f.w: the Spirit of the LORD shall carry thee

chapters.n: Obadiah points to his record of secretly saving the hundred prophets.
For the third time he repeats the command, voicing his fear.
Elijah swears by the “LORD of hosts”—the Lord of heaven’s armies—that he will face Ahab today.

f.g: Jehovah Sabaoth: the Lord of armies, heavenly and earthly.

chapters.n: Obadiah delivers the message, and Ahab goes to meet Elijah.
Ahab calls Elijah the “troubler of Israel,” blaming him for the drought.

f.g: brings disaster upon; the same word used of Achan.

chapters.n: Elijah turns the charge around: Ahab and his family brought this disaster by forsaking the Lord and following the Baals.

f.g: plural of Baal: the various local forms of Baal worship.

chapters.n: Elijah demands a public contest on Mount Carmel with 450 prophets of Baal and 400 of Asherah, all supported by Jezebel.

f.g: a mountain ridge by the Mediterranean coast, on the border with Phoenicia.
prophets of Asherah, the mother-goddess.

chapters.n: Ahab complies and gathers the people and the prophets.
Elijah confronts the people: How long will you limp back and forth between two choices? Choose! Their silence shows their divided hearts.

f.g: limp, waver—literally ‘hop’ between two branches.

chapters.n: Elijah stresses the odds: one prophet of the Lord against 450 of Baal.
He proposes the test: each side prepares a bull on wood, but no one lights the fire.

f.g: young bulls.
prepare.

chapters.n: The God who answers with fire is the true God. Since Baal was hailed as the lord of storm and lightning, this was a test on his own ground. The people agree.
Elijah lets Baal’s prophets go first, since they are many.
From morning until noon they cry, “O Baal, hear us,” limping around the altar in ritual dance. No answer comes.

f.g: the same Hebrew word as ‘halt’ in verse 21—a limping dance.

chapters.n: At noon Elijah mocks them: perhaps Baal is busy, has stepped away, is traveling, or is asleep. The satire exposes how lifeless the idol is.

f.g: possibly a polite way of saying he has gone to relieve himself.

chapters.n: They shout louder and slash themselves with knives until blood flows—a pagan ritual the law forbade.

f.g: spears or sharp points.

chapters.n: They rave on until the evening sacrifice, mid-afternoon. Three times the text says there was no answer.

f.g: here, raved in a frenzy.
the daily afternoon offering, about 3 p.m.

chapters.n: Elijah calls the people close and repairs the Lord’s ruined altar—symbolically restoring true worship.

f.g: an old altar of the Lord, torn down during the persecution.

chapters.n: He uses twelve stones for the twelve tribes, reminding the divided nation that it is still one covenant people.
He builds the altar and digs a large trench around it.

f.g: the area sown by about two seahs of seed, or a trench holding that volume.

chapters.n: He prepares the sacrifice and orders four large jars of water poured over it—in a drought, a costly offering.

f.g: large water jars.

chapters.n: Three times they drench it—twelve jars in all—ruling out any trickery.
Water soaks the altar and fills the trench.
At the hour of the evening sacrifice, Elijah offers a short, calm prayer to the God of the patriarchs, asking that the Lord show Himself as Israel’s God and confirm Elijah as His servant.

f.w: LORD God of Abraham, Isaac, and of Israel

chapters.n: His deepest desire is that the people may know the Lord and that their hearts may turn back. Malachi later prophesies Elijah’s return to turn hearts, fulfilled in the restoration of sealing keys.
Fire from the Lord falls and consumes everything—offering, wood, stones, dust, and water. Nothing is left.

f.w: the fire of the LORD fell

chapters.n: The people fall to the ground and cry, “The LORD, he is the God!”—a confession that echoes Elijah’s own name: “My God is Jehovah.”

f.w: The LORD, he is the God

chapters.n: Elijah orders the false prophets seized and executed at the Kishon brook, carrying out the law’s penalty for leading Israel into idolatry.

f.g: a stream flowing past Mount Carmel to the sea.

chapters.n: Elijah tells Ahab to go eat; he already hears the sound of coming rain by faith, before any cloud appears.
Ahab feasts; Elijah prays, bowed low with his face between his knees.

f.w: put his face between his knees
f.g: a posture of intense, humble prayer.

chapters.n: Elijah sends his servant to look toward the sea seven times. Even a great prophet keeps praying persistently.
On the seventh look, a cloud as small as a hand appears. Elijah warns Ahab to hurry home before the storm traps him.

f.g: a tiny sign that faith recognizes as the beginning of a great blessing.

chapters.n: The sky darkens and heavy rain finally falls. Ahab drives his chariot to his palace at Jezreel.

f.g: a royal city in the Jezreel Valley, about 17 miles east of Carmel.

chapters.n: Empowered by the Lord, Elijah tucks up his robe and outruns Ahab’s chariot to Jezreel—an extraordinary display of divine strength.

f.g: God’s power resting on someone.
tucked his long robe into his belt to run freely.

chapters.n: Ahab reports the events on Carmel to Jezebel, focusing not on the Lord’s fire but on the death of her prophets.

f.g: also, in addition.

chapters.n: Jezebel swears an oath to kill Elijah within a day. Interestingly, she sends a warning rather than soldiers—perhaps hoping to drive him away and discredit him.

f.w: So let the gods do to me, and more also
f.g: a standard oath formula: ‘May the gods punish me severely if I fail.’

chapters.n: After his great victory, Elijah flees for his life about a hundred miles south to Beersheba, at Judah’s southern edge, and leaves his servant there.

f.g: a town at the southern boundary of Judah; ‘from Dan to Beersheba’ meant the whole land.

chapters.n: Alone in the desert under a broom tree, Elijah asks to die. Exhausted and discouraged, he feels he has failed like those before him. Even great prophets experience despair—and God meets them there.

f.g: a desert broom shrub (Hebrew rotem), giving thin shade.

chapters.n: While he sleeps, an angel touches him and tells him to eat. God’s first answer to despair is rest and nourishment, not rebuke.
Bread baked on hot stones and a jar of water are waiting at his head. He eats and sleeps again.

f.g: baked on hot stones.
a jar or jug.

chapters.n: The angel returns, recognizing that the journey ahead is too much for Elijah on his own strength.

f.g: a heavenly messenger acting on the Lord’s behalf.

chapters.n: Strengthened by that food, Elijah travels forty days and nights to Horeb (Mount Sinai). Like Moses, he goes to the mountain of God, fasting forty days—a pattern Jesus would also follow.

f.g: another name for Mount Sinai.
food.

chapters.n: At Horeb he spends the night in a cave—perhaps the very cleft where Moses saw the Lord’s glory. The Lord asks him a searching question: “What are you doing here?”

f.g: Hebrew ‘the cave,’ suggesting a known place.

chapters.n: Elijah pours out his grievance: he has been zealous for the Lord, Israel has broken its covenant, the prophets are dead, and he alone is left.

f.g: zealous, passionately devoted.

f.w: I, even I only, am left

chapters.n: The Lord tells him to stand on the mountain. A violent wind shatters rocks, then an earthquake shakes the ground—but the Lord is not in either. These were the dramatic signs of Sinai.

Then fire—but the Lord is not in it either. Then comes a “still small voice,” a gentle whisper. After the fire of Carmel, God teaches that His most important work is often quiet. Latter-day scripture likewise describes the Spirit as a still, small voice that pierces the soul.

f.g: Hebrew qol demamah daqqah: ‘a sound of thin silence’ or ‘a gentle whisper.’

chapters.n: Hearing the voice, Elijah covers his face with his cloak in reverence and steps to the cave’s entrance. The Lord asks again, “What are you doing here, Elijah?”

f.w: wrapped his face in his mantle

f.g: a prophet’s outer cloak, later a symbol of his authority.

chapters.n: Elijah repeats his complaint word for word. His feelings haven’t changed yet, but the Lord will now give him a new mission.
God’s answer is work to do. He sends Elijah to anoint Hazael as king of Aram (Syria), who would become a scourge on unfaithful Israel.

f.g: set apart by pouring oil; here perhaps meaning to designate or appoint.

chapters.n: He is also to anoint Jehu as Israel’s next king and Elisha as his own successor. These were fulfilled partly by Elisha and his disciples.

f.g: ‘God is salvation.’
in your place, as your successor.

chapters.n: These three—Hazael, Jehu, and Elisha—would carry out the Lord’s judgments on Baal worship.

f.g: Elisha’s ‘sword’ was mostly his prophetic word.

chapters.n: Elijah is not alone after all: the Lord has preserved seven thousand faithful people who never bowed to Baal or kissed his image. God always has a faithful remnant.

f.g: kissing an idol or kissing toward it was an act of worship.

chapters.n: Elijah finds Elisha plowing with the last of twelve teams of oxen—a sign of a prosperous family. Throwing his cloak over Elisha was a symbolic call to discipleship and succession.

f.g: twelve pairs, showing the family’s wealth.

chapters.n: Elisha asks only to say goodbye to his parents. Elijah’s reply—“Go back; what have I done to you?”—leaves the choice with Elisha. Compare the Savior’s teaching about putting the hand to the plow.

f.w: Let me, I pray thee, kiss my father and my mother

chapters.n: Elisha slaughters his oxen, burns his plowing gear to cook them, and feeds the people. With nothing to return to, he follows Elijah and becomes his servant. True discipleship burns the bridges back to the old life.

f.g: the wooden yokes and plow.
served him as an assistant.

chapters.n: Ben-hadad II of Aram (Syria) besieges Samaria with a coalition of thirty-two vassal kings or chieftains. Israel’s capital is surrounded.

f.g: likely Ben-hadad II, king of Aram-Damascus; ‘son of (the god) Hadad.’
army.

chapters.n: He sends envoys into the city with his demands.
His demand is total: Ahab’s silver, gold, wives, and finest children belong to Ben-hadad.

f.g: the best, most attractive.

chapters.n: Ahab submits, treating it as a formal statement of vassal loyalty: “I am yours.”
Ben-hadad sends a second, harsher message, clarifying what he meant.
Now he will send men to search Ahab’s palace and the homes of his officials and take whatever they value. This is open humiliation and plunder.

f.g: precious to you.

chapters.n: Ahab consults the elders, pointing out that Ben-hadad is looking for trouble.

f.g: take note, pay attention.
harm, trouble.

chapters.n: The elders and people advise him to refuse.
Ahab agrees to the first terms but rejects the second.
Ben-hadad boasts that his army is so huge that Samaria’s dust wouldn’t give each soldier a handful—he will grind the city to powder.

f.w: The gods do so unto me, and more also
f.g: an oath formula: ‘May the gods punish me if I fail.’

chapters.n: Ahab answers with a proverb: a soldier putting on his armor shouldn’t boast like one taking it off after victory. In other words, don’t celebrate before the battle.

f.g: armor.

chapters.n: Ben-hadad, drinking with his allies in their tents, orders his troops into battle positions.

f.g: temporary shelters or booths.
take up battle positions.

chapters.n: Unexpectedly, a prophet comes to wicked Ahab with a promise of victory, so that Ahab will know the Lord is God. God’s mercy reaches even an unfaithful king.

f.w: thou shalt know that I am the LORD

chapters.n: The Lord will use the young officers of the district governors, and Ahab himself will lead the attack.

f.g: begin or lead the battle.
district governors.

chapters.n: Ahab’s forces are tiny: 232 young officers and 7,000 soldiers—the same number as the faithful remnant in chapter 19.
They attack at noon while Ben-hadad and his allies are drunk.
The young officers lead the way, and Ben-hadad’s scouts report them.
Overconfident, Ben-hadad orders them captured alive whether they come for peace or war.
The small force advances with the army behind it.
Each Israelite kills his opponent, the Arameans panic and flee, and Ben-hadad escapes on horseback.
Ahab joins the pursuit, striking the horses and chariots and winning a great victory.
The prophet warns Ahab to prepare, because Aram will attack again next spring, the season when kings went to war.

f.w: at the return of the year
f.g: next spring, the usual campaign season.

chapters.n: Ben-hadad’s advisers explain the defeat theologically: Israel’s gods must be mountain gods, so fight them on the plain. Ancient peoples often thought gods had limited territories.

f.g: many ancient peoples believed each god ruled a particular region.

chapters.n: They also advise replacing the vassal kings with professional military commanders.

f.g: in their places.

chapters.n: Rebuild an army equal to the one lost and fight on flat ground. Ben-hadad agrees.
The next spring Ben-hadad marches to Aphek, probably east of the Sea of Galilee, on level terrain.

f.g: a common place name; this one was likely east of the Sea of Galilee.

chapters.n: Israel’s army looks like two small flocks of goats compared to the Arameans, who fill the countryside.

f.g: young goats.

chapters.n: Because the Arameans claimed the Lord was only a god of the hills, He will give Israel the victory to prove He is God everywhere.

f.w: he is not God of the valleys

chapters.n: After a seven-day standoff, battle is joined and Israel strikes down a vast number of Aramean foot soldiers. Large numbers in ancient texts may reflect military units rather than exact counts.

f.g: infantry soldiers.

chapters.n: Survivors flee into Aphek, where a wall collapses on many more. Ben-hadad hides in an inner room.

f.g: literally ‘a room within a room,’ a hiding place.

chapters.n: Ben-hadad’s officials suggest begging for mercy, having heard Israel’s kings are merciful. They wear sackcloth and ropes as signs of surrender and submission.

f.g: coarse cloth worn in mourning or humility.
a sign of surrender, as captives with ropes on their necks.

chapters.n: They plead for Ben-hadad’s life. Ahab calls him “my brother”—a term for a treaty equal—shockingly friendly toward the enemy God had delivered to him.

f.g: treaty language for an ally of equal rank.

chapters.n: The servants seize on Ahab’s word as a hopeful sign. Ahab invites Ben-hadad into his royal chariot, a sign of honor.

f.g: quickly took it as an omen and held him to it.

chapters.n: Ben-hadad offers to return captured towns and grant Israel trading quarters in Damascus. Ahab makes a treaty and lets him go—putting political advantage ahead of God’s command.

f.w: make streets for thee in Damascus
f.g: set up market districts or trading quarters.

chapters.n: One of the “sons of the prophets”—members of a prophetic community—asks a companion, by the Lord’s word, to strike him. The companion refuses.

f.g: a fellowship or school of prophets, often led by Elijah or Elisha.

chapters.n: Because he refused a command given by the Lord’s word, a lion kills him—echoing the man of God in chapter 13. The story stresses that Ahab will be judged for his own disobedience.
Another man strikes the prophet and wounds him, as needed for the coming parable.
The prophet waits by the road disguised with a bandage over his eyes (or ashes) to look like a wounded soldier.

f.g: or ‘a bandage over his eyes’; the Hebrew word is uncertain.

chapters.n: He tells the king a made-up story: he was told to guard a prisoner on pain of death or a huge fine.

chapters.n: While he was busy, the prisoner escaped. Ahab declares that the soldier has pronounced his own sentence—just as David did when Nathan told his parable.

f.g: Hebrew herem: devoted to God, under the ban.

chapters.n: Ahab returns to Samaria sullen and angry—not repentant. The same words describe him in the next chapter.

f.g: sullen and resentful.

chapters.n: Naboth, a man of Jezreel, owns a vineyard right next to Ahab’s palace there. Ahab ruled from Samaria but kept a second residence at Jezreel.

f.g: right next to.
a royal city overlooking the fertile Jezreel Valley.

chapters.n: Ahab offers a fair trade or a cash price so he can turn the vineyard into a vegetable garden. On the surface, the offer seems reasonable.

f.g: a vegetable garden.

chapters.n: Naboth refuses on religious grounds. Under the law of Moses, family land was a sacred inheritance from the Lord, not to be permanently sold.

f.g: an oath: ‘God forbid that I should do this.’

chapters.n: Ahab goes home sulking like a spoiled child—lying on his bed, face to the wall, refusing to eat.
Jezebel asks why he is so upset.
Ahab retells the story but leaves out Naboth’s reason—that the land was his family inheritance from God.
Jezebel mocks him: “Aren’t you the king?” In her Phoenician view, a king simply takes what he wants. She promises to get the vineyard herself.

f.w: Dost thou now govern the kingdom of Israel?
f.g: possibly sarcastic: ‘Is this how you act as king?’

chapters.n: She writes letters in Ahab’s name, seals them with his royal seal, and sends them to the leaders of Naboth’s town. Ahab’s seal makes him complicit.

f.g: stamped with the king’s signet, giving them royal authority.

chapters.n: She orders a public fast—normally called in times of crisis or to address sin—and has Naboth seated in a prominent place, setting him up for an accusation.

f.g: seat him in a prominent place before the assembly.

chapters.n: Two false witnesses—the minimum the law required—will accuse him of cursing God and the king, a capital crime. Then he is to be stoned.

f.g: worthless, wicked men; scoundrels.

chapters.n: The town’s leaders obey Jezebel’s instructions—a chilling picture of officials who go along with injustice out of fear or self-interest.
They proclaim the fast and seat Naboth in front.
The two scoundrels accuse Naboth publicly, and he is taken outside the town and stoned. Second Kings adds that his sons were killed too, ending any heir’s claim.

f.g: good-for-nothings, scoundrels.

chapters.n: The elders report back to Jezebel: Naboth is dead.
Jezebel tells Ahab to go take the vineyard, since Naboth is dead.
Ahab asks no questions and goes to claim it.
God has seen everything. His word comes to Elijah.
Elijah is sent to confront Ahab in the very vineyard he is claiming.
Elijah’s indictment is sharp: “Have you murdered and also taken possession?” Ahab’s blood will be licked up by dogs just as Naboth’s was.
Ahab greets him, “So you’ve found me, my enemy!” Elijah answers that Ahab has sold himself—like a slave—to do evil.

f.g: given yourself over completely, like a slave sold to a master.

chapters.n: Ahab’s whole dynasty will be wiped out, every male.

f.w: him that pisseth against the wall
f.g: a crude idiom for every male.

chapters.n: His house will end like Jeroboam’s and Baasha’s.
Jezebel too will die disgracefully, eaten by dogs near the wall of Jezreel—fulfilled about fifteen years later.
Like Jeroboam’s and Baasha’s families, Ahab’s relatives will lie unburied.
The narrator adds a summary verdict: no one was as wicked as Ahab, urged on by Jezebel.

f.g: incited, provoked.

chapters.n: His idolatry made him like the Amorites, the Canaanite peoples the Lord had driven out of the land.
Surprisingly, Ahab responds with genuine sorrow—tearing his clothes, wearing sackcloth, fasting, and walking quietly in mourning.

f.g: tore his garments, a sign of grief or repentance.
walked quietly, subdued, as a mourner.

chapters.n: The Lord speaks to Elijah again.
The Lord notices even the humility of a very wicked man and delays the disaster to his son’s days. This shows how readily God responds to repentance—though the judgment on the dynasty still stands.

f.w: Seest thou how Ahab humbleth himself

chapters.n: After Ahab’s treaty with Ben-hadad, three years of peace follow between Aram and Israel. Assyrian records suggest the two even fought side by side against Assyria at Qarqar in 853 BC.
Jehoshaphat, the righteous king of Judah, visits Ahab. The two kingdoms are now allied, sealed by the marriage of Jehoshaphat’s son to Ahab’s daughter.

f.g: traveled north from Jerusalem’s heights; ‘down’ in elevation.

chapters.n: Ahab complains that Ramoth-gilead, an important fortress town east of the Jordan, is still held by Aram—apparently one of the cities Ben-hadad had promised to return.

f.g: a fortified city east of the Jordan and a city of refuge.
we sit idle, doing nothing.

chapters.n: Ahab invites Jehoshaphat to join the campaign, and Jehoshaphat commits fully: “I am as you are.” Chronicles records that a prophet later rebuked him for this alliance.
Jehoshaphat wisely insists on seeking the Lord’s will first.

f.g: seek an answer from God through a prophet.

chapters.n: Ahab gathers about four hundred court prophets, who all say, “Go up.” They speak of “the Lord” (Adonai), not clearly naming Jehovah, and they tell the king what he wants to hear.

f.g: hold back, refrain.
here Hebrew Adonai, a general title, rather than the covenant name Jehovah (LORD).

chapters.n: Jehoshaphat senses something is wrong and asks whether there is a true prophet of the LORD available.
Ahab admits there is one, Micaiah, but hates him because he never prophesies good for Ahab. Jehoshaphat gently objects.

f.g: ‘Who is like Jehovah?’

chapters.n: Ahab sends an officer to bring Micaiah quickly.

f.g: a court official, perhaps a eunuch.

chapters.n: The two kings sit enthroned in royal robes at Samaria’s city gate, the public square of an ancient town, while the prophets perform.

f.g: an open area, a threshing floor.

chapters.n: Zedekiah, one of the court prophets, makes iron horns to act out the prophecy: Ahab will gore the Arameans like a bull.

f.g: horns symbolize strength and power.
gore, as an ox does with its horns.

chapters.n: All the prophets repeat the same encouraging message.
The messenger urges Micaiah to agree with the others—pressure to conform.

f.g: unanimously.

chapters.n: Micaiah refuses: he will speak only what the Lord tells him. This is the mark of a true prophet.

f.w: what the LORD saith unto me, that will I speak

chapters.n: At first Micaiah repeats the court prophets’ words—apparently with obvious sarcasm, since Ahab immediately sees through it.
Ahab demands the truth. Ironically, he insists on hearing what he has already decided to ignore.

f.g: put under oath, solemnly command.

chapters.n: Micaiah describes a vision: Israel scattered on the hills like sheep without a shepherd. In other words, the king will die, and his army will go home leaderless.

f.w: as sheep that have not a shepherd

chapters.n: Ahab turns to Jehoshaphat: “Didn’t I tell you?”
Micaiah reveals a heavenly council: the Lord enthroned and surrounded by the armies of heaven. Prophets often describe being shown God’s council.

f.w: I saw the LORD sitting on his throne

f.g: the heavenly beings attending God.

chapters.n: The Lord asks who will entice Ahab to go to his death at Ramoth-gilead. The council discusses ideas.

f.g: entice, lure.

chapters.n: A spirit steps forward and volunteers.

Micaiah declares plainly that the four hundred prophets are deceived, and disaster is decreed for Ahab.
Zedekiah slaps Micaiah and sneers, “Which way did the Spirit of the Lord go from me to you?”
Micaiah answers that Zedekiah will find out when he is hiding in an inner room in terror after the defeat.
Ahab orders Micaiah handed over to the city governor and a royal prince.

f.g: meager prison rations.
safely, victoriously.

f.w: If thou return at all in peace

chapters.n: Both kings march on Ramoth-gilead anyway—even Jehoshaphat, who had heard the warning.
Ahab tries to cheat the prophecy by disguising himself as an ordinary soldier, while Jehoshaphat wears his royal robes—making Jehoshaphat the obvious target.
Ben-hadad orders his chariot commanders to target only the king of Israel. Ahab’s release of him three years earlier now comes back to haunt him.
Seeing Jehoshaphat’s royal robes, the chariots chase him. Jehoshaphat cries out—Chronicles adds that he cried to the Lord, who helped him.
Realizing he isn’t Ahab, they stop the pursuit.
An archer shoots at random, yet the arrow strikes Ahab precisely in the gap between his armor plates. No disguise can hide a man from God’s word.

f.g: at random, without aiming at anyone in particular.

f.w: between the joints of the harness
f.g: between the scales of his armor and the breastplate.

chapters.n: Ahab is propped up in his chariot all day to keep up morale, and dies at evening as his blood pools in the chariot.

f.g: held up, propped up.

chapters.n: At sunset the call goes out: “Every man to his home.” Israel is scattered, just as Micaiah saw.

f.w: the dogs licked up his blood

f.g: the Hebrew likely means ‘and the harlots washed themselves there.’

chapters.n: Ahab’s building works included an “ivory house”—a palace decorated with ivory inlays. Archaeologists have found many carved ivories at Samaria.
Ahab dies; his son Ahaziah succeeds him.
The narrator now summarizes Jehoshaphat’s reign in Judah.
He was thirty-five at his accession and ruled twenty-five years (about 873–848 BC, including a co-regency with his father).
Jehoshaphat followed his father Asa’s good example, though local shrines remained in use.

chapters.n: He ended the long hostility between Judah and Israel, partly through marriage alliance with Ahab’s family—a decision that would later bring Baal worship into Judah.

f.w: made peace with the king of Israel

chapters.n: Chronicles records much more of his reign, including his teaching program and judicial reforms.
He completed his father’s reform by removing the remaining shrine prostitutes.

f.g: cult prostitutes.

chapters.n: Edom was then governed by a deputy under Judah’s control, which gave Judah access to the Red Sea port.

f.g: a governor appointed by Judah served as ruler.

chapters.n: Jehoshaphat tried to revive Solomon’s gold trade with Ophir, but his ships were wrecked in port at Ezion-geber. Chronicles says it was a judgment for allying with Ahab’s son.

f.g: large ocean-going trading ships.

chapters.n: Ahaziah of Israel offered to send his sailors too, but Jehoshaphat refused—perhaps having learned his lesson.
Jehoshaphat dies and his son Jehoram becomes king of Judah.
Ahab’s son Ahaziah begins a short two-year reign over Israel (about 853–852 BC).
He followed in the ways of his father Ahab, his mother Jezebel, and Jeroboam—three generations of false worship.
He served Baal as his father had. His story continues in 2 Kings 1, where he seeks a foreign god even on his sickbed.
